newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Discouraged workers cause Australian jobless dip.
newsitem.headline: Discouraged workers cause Australian jobless dip.

text.p: The apparently good news of a large drop in Australian unemployment in June is in fact a reflection of the weak state of the labour market as discouraged workers give up the search for work, analysts said.
Australia's unemployment rate dropped to 8.5 percent in June, its lowest level since last November, from 8.8 percent in May as employment rose 11,900, official data on Thursay showed.
But that employment rise did little to reverse May's 40,300 fall, and meant the number of employed people had actually fallen in the first half of 1997.
The weakness in the data was supportive of market sentiment that another interest rate cut was likely from the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) in the near future.
"It looks like a fairly weak set of numbers to me," SBC Warburg senior economist Guy Bruten said.
"A rise of 11,900 overall -- a lot weaker than the markets were looking for and gives you a fairly weak picture over the last six months," he said.
While the government welcomed the unemployment drop, with employment Minister Amanda Vanstone saying job market signs were positive, analysts said the cause of the drop was a concern.

"The participation rate fall to 63.0 percent is the lowest in three years, so that suggests to me a mounting discouraged worker effect and that's the only reason why the unemployment rate came back," UBS chief economist Stephen Roberts said.

The inability of the economy to generate jobs growth had so discouraged job seekers that they had left the workforce -- the participation rate fell to a three year low of 63.0 percent in June, down from 63.2 percent in May and 63.5 percent in April.
The participation rate measures the labour force -- employed people and unemployed people looking for work -- as a percentage of the working age population.
While the working age population has increased by 34,400 in the past two months, the labour force has fallen by 52,900.
"Had the participation rate been at the April level of 63.5 percent, the June unemployment rate would have been over 9.0 percent," Westpac senior economist John Peters said.
Although the falling participation rate was helpful to the unemployment rate, it could do little to hide the picture of a still soft jobs market.
Total employment actually fell by 4,000 in the first half of 1997. More worrying for analysts was the ongoing weakness in full-time employment.

Full time jobs have fallen by 40,000 in the past two months, and by 63,900 in the first half of 1997. Full-time jobs are seen as having more flow-through effects to the economy as they pay more and are considered more long term than part-time jobs.
Some economists, however, saw the ongoing weakness in full-time employment as a result of a deregulated labour market producing a more flexible and mobile labour force.

"It's not just the last six months, we've undergone a gradual restructuring of the workforce over the last few years away from full-time work towards part-time," Dresdner Australia chief economist Rob Henderson said.
But regardless of how they saw the split between full-time and part-time employment, economists generally agreed the labour market was weak and increased chances of a near term rate cut.

While a Friday cut was a chance, most said an easing would be held off until after wages and inflation data were released in two weeks, or after the RBA's August 5 board meeting, so the cut could be sold on the good news of low inflation.

"It is possible that they may go tomorrow (Friday), but I think that it's more likely that they'll wait until after the inflation and wages data," ANZ Treasury senior economist David de Garis said. -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
